narrative:
The model predicted a 65% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability exceeded the school's acceptance threshold, your law school application was denied.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors from your academic record. Your class ranking at the end of your third year was the strongest influence and pushed the prediction toward failure. While most accepted students ranked around the 6th decile, you placed in the 3rd decile, signaling weaker performance relative to your peers at that stage. Your first-year ranking also worked against you, though to a lesser degree; you stood in the 3rd decile compared with an average of 6th among accepted applicants.

Your LSAT score was the second most important factor and worked in your favor. At 39, it sat above the 37.2 average of accepted students and pulled the prediction toward passing. Unfortunately, this positive signal was not strong enough to overcome the negative impact of your class rankings.

Your family income, undergraduate GPA of 3.3, full-time status, gender, and race played no meaningful role in the outcome.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic trajectory. Raising your class rank in future years or demonstrating consistent improvement could significantly shift future predictions in your favor. Consider reapplying once you have additional evidence of stronger performance.
